what_its_for: Oxymorphone is a strong prescription pain medicine (opioid) used to treat moderate to severe pain that is not well controlled by other pain medicines. The extended-release tablets are used around the clock for ongoing pain that needs long-term treatment.
how_to_take: Take oxymorphone exactly as your doctor prescribed. Swallow tablets whole — do not crush, chew, dissolve, snort, or inject them, as this can cause a dangerous overdose or death. Take it on an EMPTY stomach, at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after eating, because food can cause too much medicine to enter your body at once. Do not drink alcohol while taking this medicine. Do not stop taking it suddenly without talking to your doctor first, as this can cause withdrawal symptoms.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on the lowest dose that controls your pain and adjust it based on how you respond. For immediate-release tablets, the typical starting dose for adults is 5 to 20 mg every 4 to 6 hours as needed. For extended-release tablets, dosing is usually every 12 hours. Never take more than prescribed, and never take doses closer together than directed. Everyone's dose is different — do not share this medicine with anyone.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose of the immediate-release tablet, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and take the next one at the regular time. For extended-release tablets, if you miss a dose, skip it and take the next scheduled dose. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one, as this could cause a dangerous overdose.
storage: Store oxymorphone at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it in a safe, secure location away from children and pets. Do not store it in a bathroom where it can be affected by moisture and heat. Dispose of any unused medicine safely — do not flush unless the label says to or your pharmacist advises it. Use a drug take-back program if available.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol in any form — including beer, wine, liquor, or alcohol-containing cough syrups — as it can cause life-threatening breathing problems. Do not drive, operate heavy machinery, or do anything requiring full alertness until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid taking sleeping pills, anti-anxiety medicines, muscle relaxers, or other opioid pain medicines without your doctor's knowledge, as these combinations can be deadly. Do not take sedatives, benzodiazepines (like Xanax or Valium), or any other central nervous system depressants without your doctor's approval.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or get emergency help immediately if you experience: very slow, shallow, or stopped breathing; extreme drowsiness or difficulty waking up; lips, fingernails, or skin turning blue; severe dizziness or fainting; chest pain; seizures; signs of a severe allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing; signs of adrenal problems such as nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, or extreme weakness; or if you feel the medicine is no longer working as well. Also call your doctor if you feel dependent on the medicine or if you are taking more than prescribed. Keep naloxone (Narcan) on hand in case of an overdose emergency.
when_it_works: Immediate-release oxymorphone usually starts working within 30 to 60 minutes after you take it and provides pain relief for about 4 to 6 hours. Extended-release oxymorphone begins working within 1 to 2 hours and is designed to provide steady pain relief over 12 hours. You may not feel the full effect of extended-release tablets for several days as your body adjusts to the medicine.
special_populations: Elderly patients (65 and older): Start at the lowest possible dose and be closely monitored, as older adults are more sensitive to opioids and at higher risk for breathing problems, falls, and confusion. Pregnancy: Do not take this medicine during pregnancy unless absolutely necessary — it can cause life-threatening withdrawal in a newborn baby. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed while taking oxymorphone, as it passes into breast milk and can harm your baby. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose or avoid this medicine altogether. Children: Oxymorphone is not approved for use in children.
